summaries.headline: Districts Find Success Through Personal Outreach on Absenteeism
summaries.summary: School leaders are discovering that addressing chronic absenteeism requires moving beyond policy enforcement to understanding the individual circumstances keeping students away from school. Districts implementing human-centered approaches focus on building relationships with families, identifying specific barriers like transportation or health issues, and providing targeted support rather than punitive measures. The shift toward personalized intervention strategies reflects growing recognition that attendance challenges often stem from complex family and community factors that traditional disciplinary responses cannot address.

summaries.headline: Education Department Dissolves Office Serving English Learners
summaries.summary: The Education Department is dissolving the Office of English Language Acquisition, which supports the country's 5 million English learners, as part of the Trump administration's broader plan to dismantle the department and eliminate federal funding for English language programs. The office already faced decimation through early layoffs, and the department quietly rescinded key guidance last August that states and districts used to protect immigrant student rights. Officials claim integrating English learner services across other department offices will reduce administrative burden, though the move comes amid mass deportation campaigns affecting the very communities these students represent.

summaries.headline: Five Candidates Vie for Memphis Board Seat
summaries.summary: Five candidates are competing in Memphis-Shelby County's District 9 Democratic primary on May 5, ranging from incumbent vice chair Joyce Dorse-Coleman to the only pro-state takeover advocate on any 2026 ballot. The district serves around 12,000 students across 24 schools, with 60% economically disadvantaged and a student body that is 65% Black and one-third Hispanic. The election comes as state lawmakers advance legislation to create a board of managers that could strip local school board authority from the district.

summaries.headline: Small Districts Share Low-Cost Cybersecurity Strategies
summaries.summary: Small and midsize K-12 districts outlined practical cybersecurity approaches at the 2026 CoSN Annual Conference, focusing on strategies that work within tight budgets and limited staffing. Technology leaders emphasized starting with basic asset inventories and risk assessments, using tools as simple as spreadsheets to identify what districts have and where vulnerabilities exist. The framework addresses five core questions about cyber readiness, from knowing current assets to planning incident recovery — providing smaller districts a roadmap that doesn't require enterprise-level resources.

summaries.headline: Detroit District Accelerates Closure of Four Small Schools
summaries.summary: The Detroit Public Schools Community District will close four underenrolled schools at the end of this school year, accelerating a phase-out plan originally set to unfold gradually over several years. The schools — Ann Arbor Trail Magnet School, J.E. Clark Preparatory Academy, Catherine Blackwell Institute, and Greenfield Union Elementary-Middle School — were identified for closure in 2022 due to low enrollment and high operating costs, but Superintendent Nikolai Vitti cited budget pressures and anticipated federal funding cuts as reasons for the faster timeline. The compressed closure schedule underscores how financial constraints are forcing districts to make abrupt decisions that may leave families with little time to plan transitions.

summaries.headline: CoSN Report Maps Staff Shortages, Security as Innovation Barriers
summaries.summary: The Consortium for School Networking's 2026 report, compiled by 130 advisors from 14 countries, identifies staffing challenges and cybersecurity concerns as the top hurdles blocking K-12 technology innovation. District leaders at the CoSN conference emphasized that empowerment through purpose-driven work, professional growth opportunities, and flexible schedules helps retain both instructional and IT staff. The findings suggest that districts treating technology implementation as a human capital challenge—not just a procurement issue—may have better success navigating both security demands and innovation goals.

summaries.headline: Adobe Expands AI Tools for K-12 Education
summaries.summary: Adobe is significantly expanding its AI-powered tools and training resources designed specifically for K-12 educators and students, positioning AI as a catalyst for creativity rather than a replacement for critical thinking. The company offers site and district licenses for Creative Cloud's 20+ digital media apps with generative AI capabilities, plus free access to Adobe Express for Education with built-in AI tools designed for classroom safety. Districts building AI literacy now through hands-on experience with industry-standard tools are positioning students for a workforce where AI proficiency has become table stakes.

summaries.headline: Denver Committee Recommends Bell-to-Bell Phone Ban
summaries.summary: Denver Public Schools could adopt a comprehensive cellphone ban after a 17-member community committee recommended prohibiting smartphones, smartwatches, and earbuds from start to finish of the school day. The committee's proposal includes making devices completely inaccessible during school hours, with exceptions only for medical needs or disability accommodations, and suggests linking teacher evaluations to consistent policy enforcement. The recommendation comes as Colorado's largest district with more than 89,000 students faces a July 1 deadline to establish cellphone policies under new state law, joining a growing number of districts nationwide grappling with technology's role in classroom focus and student mental health.

summaries.headline: Newark Lawmaker Pushes Back on GOP School Scrutiny
summaries.summary: Assembly Budget Chair Eliana Pintor Marin criticized Republican lawmakers for repeatedly targeting Newark schools' spending during a heated state budget hearing, calling the focus "reductive" and saying she's "tired of it." GOP legislators questioned the district's expenditures on AI surveillance systems, COVID relief tutoring, and a controversial elementary school lease, with one assemblymember saying "we should all be offended" by student outcomes despite the millions spent. The partisan clash reflects broader tensions over New Jersey's school funding formula, with Republicans targeting urban districts partly in response to funding cuts that have hit their suburban constituencies.

summaries.headline: Colorado Considers Cutting Generous Homeschool Enrichment Funding
summaries.summary: Colorado lawmakers are scrutinizing the state's $100 million annual spending on publicly funded homeschool enrichment programs, which has expanded beyond traditional academics to include horseback riding, soccer camps, and martial arts classes run by private contractors with minimal oversight. Many programs operate just six hours weekly while receiving payment for double that amount, prompting legislators to call the practice "staggering" and consider cutting rates in half amid the state's $1.2 billion budget shortfall. The funding debate reflects broader tensions over public education resources as traditional school districts face enrollment declines and competing priorities for shrinking state dollars.

summaries.headline: Canva Launches AI Platform Targeting Classroom Workflows
summaries.summary: Canva has released AI 2.0, transforming from a design tool into an AI-driven platform that generates complete content from conversational prompts and integrates with education workflows. The update includes Learn Grid, which allows teachers to automatically create differentiated lesson versions, plus connectors to platforms like Google Drive, Slack, and Zoom that pull existing communications into editable classroom materials. The move positions Canva as a comprehensive workspace where educators can plan, create, and deliver instruction within a single platform rather than managing multiple disconnected tools.

summaries.headline: Microsoft Research Fellows Target AI Impact in Education
summaries.summary: Microsoft Research announced its 2026 Fellowship cohort with several projects examining how artificial intelligence affects employment, skills development, and classroom applications. The global group includes researchers studying AI adoption's impact on hiring and performance outcomes, along with work on interactive AI tools and human-AI collaboration in learning environments. The breadth of research signals a growing focus on moving AI from experimental technology to practical deployment in schools and workforce training programs.

summaries.headline: GoGuardian Launches EdTech Compliance Tool for Districts
summaries.summary: GoGuardian has launched Discover, a product that analyzes district technology usage data to provide compliance guidance, cost analysis, and spending recommendations ahead of budget season. The tool automatically identifies which educational technology tools districts should optimize, renew, or review, positioning itself as the only product that converts usage data into actionable board-ready decisions. Districts facing mounting pressure to justify technology investments and ensure compliance now have a centralized way to make data-driven decisions about their digital portfolios.

summaries.headline: Louisiana House Doubles Private School Funding Despite Senate Opposition
summaries.summary: The Louisiana House approved a $47 billion budget that doubles funding for the LA GATOR private school scholarship program, despite Senate leadership publicly opposing the increase. The unanimous 104-0 vote advances a spending plan that House Appropriations Chairman Jack McFarland acknowledged was driven by gubernatorial pressure, with one Democratic lawmaker noting he "would not have doubled it" but accepted the compromise. The budget's future remains uncertain as it heads to the hostile Senate and depends on voter approval of constitutional amendments that could require an additional $50 million for teacher pay or force lawmakers to find $198 million elsewhere if the measures fail.

summaries.headline: Illinois Approves New School Accountability Labels System
summaries.summary: The Illinois State Board of Education unanimously approved an overhaul of its school accountability system, replacing the current five-category labeling structure with new designations that would more evenly distribute schools across performance levels. Under the new system, 23% of K-8 schools and 29% of high schools would earn "Commendable" ratings compared to 73% of all schools under the current system, while roughly one-fifth of schools would be considered "exemplary" versus just 10% today. The changes await federal approval before taking effect this fall, though education advocacy groups remain opposed to the removal of ninth-grade on-track measures and what they consider insufficient attendance metrics.

summaries.headline: Gates County Takes Letterland Phonics Beyond Classroom Walls
summaries.summary: Gates County Schools expanded their Letterland phonics program into community spaces, with staff and volunteers dressing as letter characters at local parks and events to reinforce early literacy concepts. The district's creative approach transforms public spaces into learning environments, connecting systematic phonics instruction with real-world application and family engagement. The initiative demonstrates how districts can extend evidence-based literacy practices beyond school hours, potentially strengthening the home-school connection that research shows is critical for reading success.

summaries.headline: Tennessee House Passes Voucher Expansion Despite GOP Opposition
summaries.summary: The Tennessee House passed legislation expanding the state's voucher program to 35,000 seats in a narrow 52-43 vote, with significant Republican defections joining Democratic opposition. The bill eliminates key funding protections promised last year, removing "hold harmless" provisions that guaranteed public school funding levels regardless of enrollment losses, and quietly adds language that could enable tracking immigration status of students. Republican critics called the changes a betrayal of the original deal that secured passage of the universal voucher program just 15 months earlier.

summaries.headline: Employers Cut On-Site Child Care Despite Staff Need
summaries.summary: Universities, school districts and hospitals across the country are closing on-site child care centers that serve employee and student families, with institutions like University of Nebraska at Omaha shuttering programs that operated for decades. The closures stem from financial pressures, stagnant federal funding, and changing institutional policies that make these programs harder to sustain. The trend signals a deepening crisis in child care access that could worsen recruitment and retention challenges for education and healthcare employers already struggling with staffing shortages.

summaries.headline: Ohio District Makes Data Privacy Everyone's Job
summaries.summary: Westlake City Schools has embedded data privacy practices throughout its organizational culture rather than treating it as solely an IT responsibility, according to district officials speaking at the CoSN 2026 conference. The Ohio district emphasizes transparency in its approach, with leaders advocating against making privacy decisions "behind closed doors" and instead involving stakeholders across departments in data protection protocols. This whole-district model suggests that sustainable data privacy requires shifting from technical compliance to cultural integration, particularly as schools handle increasingly complex student information systems.

summaries.headline: Ohio Launches Statewide Attendance Dashboard to Combat Absenteeism
summaries.summary: Ohio's education department has launched a new online dashboard allowing districts to track chronic absenteeism rates in real-time across schools and student subgroups. The tool provides administrators with immediate access to attendance data that previously required manual compilation from multiple sources, enabling faster identification of students missing 10 percent or more of school days. Districts can now benchmark their performance against state averages and deploy targeted interventions before attendance patterns become entrenched academic barriers.

synthesis.topic_title: School Funding Formula Overhauls Gain Momentum as State Support Declines
synthesis.whats_happening: State lawmakers are tackling long-overdue funding formula reforms while simultaneously reducing supplemental education support. Maine completed its first major funding formula revision in 2 decades, Pennsylvania advanced budget increases through the House, and multiple states are grappling with declining state supplemental funding that shifts more financial pressure to districts.
synthesis.whats_driving: Post-pandemic fiscal pressures are forcing states to reckon with decades of deferred maintenance on funding systems while managing tighter budgets. The combination of federal relief fund expiration and persistent equity concerns is creating political urgency around formula reforms, though legislative battles are intensifying as education competes with other state priorities.

**Jake Langlais** _is superintendent of Lewiston public schools._

In Lewiston schools, we are faced with impossible choices every day. These choices aren’t about upgrades or extras, they’re about reductions in counselors, larger class sizes and no librarians to help students find the books they need. These were once the basics in public education. Now, they’re what we’re fighting to keep.

For nearly 20 years, I’ve worked in the Lewiston public school system as a coach, a teacher, a principal and now as the superintendent. My job is no longer to be in the classroom or on the field, but to make sure students have what they need to learn and grow.

Lewiston is one of Maine’s largest and most diverse school districts. Today, [roughly 70% of our students are economically disadvantaged](https://legislature.maine.gov/legis/bills/getTestimonyDoc.asp?id=184266), and many come from families who are new to our state and our country. What we are seeing in Lewiston is not unique, it’s a preview of where many communities across Maine are headed.

The problem is that our current school funding system hasn’t kept up with our changing population and student needs. Maine’s Essential Programs and Services (EPS) formula has not been meaningfully updated in nearly 20 years. It relies heavily on property values to determine a community’s ability to pay, an approach that no longer reflects the real cost of educating students or what wealth actually looks like in Maine today.

Right now, Maine legislators have an opportunity to take the first step toward fixing school funding for their communities. A current proposal, [LD 2226](https://legislature.maine.gov/legis/bills/display_ps.asp?LD=2226&snum=132), would update the EPS formula to align it more closely with what communities can afford to pay and what it actually takes to staff and support our schools.

Advertisement

For the first time, it would meaningfully incorporate community income and poverty levels into how we allocate resources, not just property wealth. This is not a rushed change. It’s the result of [two years of research](https://mepri.maine.edu/eps-study/) from the [Maine Educational Policy Research Institute](https://mepri.maine.edu/) and input from educators and communities across the state, giving us more data than ever about what our schools need and how to fund them responsibly.

As a superintendent, I’m a realist and I know there is no silver bullet to solve education overnight. Funding changes from LD 2226 will take place over time to ensure stability for all districts. It includes a [three-year hold harmless provision](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/03/19/lawmakers-advance-bill-to-reform-maines-school-funding-formula/), meaning no district will see a reduction in funding during that time, which will be followed by a two-year stable percent-based transition.

This is the kind of practical reform that reflects the reality Lewiston, like many districts, is facing: difficult budget decisions that ask us to do more with less while still supporting every student.

When schools cannot absorb those costs, the burden shifts to local taxpayers, driving up property taxes in communities that are already stretched thin. In many cases, districts cannot even fully fund essential special education services, school counselors, nurses or librarians without relying on local taxpayers to make up the difference. That’s not a failure of our schools, it’s a failure of the funding formula.

Getting here has required real compromise, and it’s paid off.

Recently, the Education Committee voted 11–2 in favor of the bill — a strong bipartisan effort that shows this is about fairness and doing right by students across the state. It reflects hard conversations and real tradeoffs. It’s not perfect, but it is thoughtful, measured and grounded in what schools actually need.

With limited time left in the session, there is a clear opportunity for Maine legislators to move this forward once and for all. Let’s not wait another 20 years to make meaningful changes for our students.

Reported by Danielle Smith, Keystone News Service

**(Harrisburg, PA)** An education advocacy group is hoping the Pennsylvania Senate will approve Governor Josh Shapiro’s proposed budget for 2026 and 2027. The Pennsylvania State Education Association says the recent passage of House Bill 2400 is a hopeful sign for schools – it contains nearly 700-million dollars to help close long‑standing funding gaps among districts. P-S-E-A President Aaron Chapin says the bipartisan measure would help the state meet its constitutional obligations. He notes this marks the third year of increased funding for Pennsylvania schools. The measure could face a tougher review in the Republican-led state Senate. Governor Josh Shapiro’s proposed 53-billion dollar spending plan requires final approval before a June 30th deadline.

Local school districts will receive $35.2 million in supplemental money for this fiscal year from the state’s Advancement and Technology Fund; however, this marks a $14.5 million decrease from last year, and future funds are uncertain.

Last week, the Alabama Legislature passed [House Bill 236](https://alison.legislature.state.al.us/files/pdf/SearchableInstruments/2026RS/HB236-enr.pdf), which detailed the allocation of these additional funds. The availability of this money depends on the state education budget operating with excess revenues. This has been the case in recent years, but state legislators have warned local schools that supplemental amounts could decrease or stop altogether in coming years, according to Decatur City Schools Superintendent Michael Douglas.

“We had, some have referred to it as, a ‘sugar high’ after COVID-19, with all the federal money, and now the revenues are reverting to the mean,” said Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, who is the Senate education budget chairman. “Year over year, we’re still positive, but the rate of increase has certainly declined. That was anticipated.”

Most local districts will receive around 30% less from this year’s Advancement and Technology disbursement than they did the previous year. Still, local education leaders stress that the funding is never guaranteed and is used toward one-time expenses.

Decatur City Schools will receive $6.6 million. Douglas said they were anticipating around $7.2 million based on previous allocations.

Last year, the district received $9.2 million. DCS purchased teacher and student devices with the appropriation, as well as 10 new school buses. It also upgraded its safety system by entrances, which includes cameras keypads for buzzing the front desk.

State law provides schools with a wide range of areas to use the money, such as deferred maintenance, new facilities, transportation, school security, technology and equipment.

“We’ve spent it on everything from school buses to Chromebooks,” Douglas said. “You can’t spend Advancement and Technology on people. Obviously, we like spending money on people to teach, but you can’t because it’s one-time, not guaranteed money. We’ve spent it on buses before. We’ve spent it on buildings. We’ve done a renovation at the Career Academies with money.”

The district will map out how it will spend this year’s allocation at a capital planning meeting, Douglas said. The funds will be factored into spending for fiscal 2027.

Limestone County Schools will receive approximately $12.4 million, a decrease from $17 million last year.

“That money is very useful for projects, especially as we’ve tried to really be aggressive with renovating our facilities and building new facilities based on need here in Limestone County,” said Superintendent Randy Shearouse. “It would certainly be missed (if not distributed in coming years). We don’t necessarily plan on receiving this funding each year. … We make plans moving forward without considering that it’s a guarantee that we’re going to receive that funding, but it certainly is a great gift to receive.”

In the past, the district has used the money for construction and renovation projects, school resource officers, insurance, utilities and fuel. Shearouse said the transportation category will be helpful given the current high cost of fuel.

Limestone County Schools will consider its [five-year capital plan](https://files-backend.assets.thrillshare.com/documents/asset/uploaded_file/4026/Lcs/9cc4c30e-986d-405d-bf78-e49f1e5e9771/2026-Capital-Plan.pdf?disposition=inline) when determining where this year’s funds will go. One of the projects the district plans to pursue is adding classrooms to Creekside Elementary School, Shearouse said. The project is estimated to cost $7.5 million, according to its capital plan.

HB236 specifies that $650,000 of this year’s Limestone allocation is to be used for athletic facility enhancements. A new gym and fieldhouse at West Limestone High School is another high-cost project included in the fiscal 2027 project list. The district is currently pursuing multiple other [athletic facilities upgrades](https://www.decaturdaily.com/news/limestone_county/limestone-schools-getting-more-than-16-million-in-improvements/article_dcb2517d-9143-47cd-8217-50d68cbf8dc7.html) across the district.

Morgan County Schools will receive $5.8 million, 37% less than last year’s $9.2 million. This is the largest decrease in the area. However, $750,000 from last year was allocated specifically for the Morgan County Agricultural Education Center.

MCS Superintendent Tracie Turrentine said in an email that, like Decatur and Limestone County, the district has used funds on safety measures.

“This year, we plan to continue the focus, with a significant portion of the funding being used to support and sustain our School Resource Officer (SRO) Program in every school,” she said. “This is extremely important to us, as student safety remains one of our top priorities. These funds will help ensure that we are able to maintain a strong law enforcement presence on each campus and continue building positive relationships between students and our SROs.”

Of this year’s appropriation, $90,000 is to be used toward an outdoor activity center at Eva Elementary School.

“This project will provide upgraded, modern playground equipment for students, creating a safer and more engaging outdoor environment,” Turrentine said.

Orr said the current equipment is around 40 to 50 years old, and he plans to help the district pursue additional funding where he can.

Hartselle City Schools will receive $2.8 million, down from $3.9 million last year. Athens City Schools was allocated $4.1 million after receiving $5.4 million last year. Lawrence County Schools was appropriated $3.5 million, down from $5 million last year.

# Letters, Week of April 15, 2026: School funding, PeaceHealth and getting back on the rails

## Send letters, maximum 250 words, to letters@cascadiadaily.com

- April 14, 2026 9:00 p.m.

By [Community Voices](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/author/community-voices/)

# LETTER OF THE WEEK

### Using foxes for crab bait is legal; it shouldn’t be

![](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%201024%20928'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Guemes Island Fire Lieutenant Mike Gregory loads a canine’s carcass into a utility vehicle after bagging and tagging it on March 31. The carcasses were later determined to be foxes used as crab bait. (Photo courtesy of Olivia Cole)

##### Editor,

Last week, approximately 25 dead foxes washed ashore on Guemes Island in Skagit County — many of them skinned, decomposed, and with their paws cut off ( [CDN, April 10, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/apr/10/canines-found-on-guemes-island-determined-to-be-foxes/)). The discovery horrified residents and baffled investigators for days. Now we know the truth, and it’s worse than anyone imagined.

The foxes were farmed outside Washington, lawfully purchased, transported into the state and intended for use as crab bait. Lawfully. Let that sink in.

Washington has no prohibition on this practice. That is a moral failure our Legislature must urgently correct.

These were sentient animals — raised in captivity, entirely dependent on human care — killed and sold as fishing bait. No animal welfare framework worth the name permits this. The fact that a boat operator could casually toss two dozen fox carcasses overboard to lighten a load — and face zero criminal charges — reveals a staggering gap in our laws.

Washington prides itself on environmental stewardship and humane values. Using farmed foxes as crab bait is incompatible with both. Olympia must pass explicit legislation banning this practice immediately, before another boatload of animals meets this fate, and before Washington’s silence becomes complicity.

The foxes that washed up on “Dog Island” deserve better. So do we.

##### Genevieve Sanchez  Bellingham

##### Editor,

From time to time, I receive a newsletter from the Bellingham School District about recent events and achievements. Only rarely do these newsletters address academic performance. Accordingly, I looked recently at state Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction Report Card data for Bellingham and four comparable districts (Everett, Olympia, Tahoma and Shoreline).

The Report Card shows how well students are performing academically in terms of meeting grade-level standards for English, mathematics and science.

Here are Bellingham’s 2025 scores: English: 70.3%, mathematics: 62.7%, science: 64%.

The averages for the other districts: English: 82.2%, mathematics: 76.3%, science: 74.2%.

There are plenty of lower-income or more-minority districts performing less well than Bellingham, but these four are our peers.

Why are Bellingham’s results so poor and what are you doing about it?

##### Roger Collier  Bellingham

##### Editor,

Offering another voice of concern: As a member of a local community service organization, I have seen firsthand the incredible resilience of our neighbors. However, the recent news of deep budget cuts hitting Whatcom County schools — including a projected $7.5 million gap in Bellingham ( [CDN, March 30, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/mar/30/bellingham-schools-to-eliminate-60-teaching-positions-due-to-budget-challenges/)) and significant staff reductions in Ferndale — is a crisis that transcends any group’s specific focus.

Our local districts are being forced to eliminate essential teaching positions, cut mental health supports and even scale back library services. These aren’t just line items on a spreadsheet; they are the resources our children need to thrive. While the state budget approved in 2025 offered some relief for special education, it remains vastly insufficient to cover the actual costs of living and inflation in our region.

The Washington State Constitution is clear: Fully funding public education is the state’s “paramount duty.” When the Legislature fails to meet this obligation, the burden falls on our local community to fill the gap or watch our schools decline.

I am writing today not as a political advocate, but as a concerned member of a community organization that values the well-being of all local families. We must urge our state leaders to prioritize a sustainable funding model that keeps pace with inflation and fully supports special education and transportation. Our children deserve more than just “surviving”; they deserve to thrive.

##### Helen Moran  Bellingham

##### Editor,

Democracy requires robust debate, so allow me to provide a counterpoint to the claims that our Legislature is underfunding our public schools.

The current “crisis” is directly attributable to the unsustainable increase in salaries following the 2018 resolution of the McCleary decision. In the 2019 school year, the average certified teacher saw a 25% increase in their real dollar salary (OSPI Report, Page 14). This constitutes the majority of the 31% increase above inflation adjustments over the last 20 years. Add this to the 19% increase in certified staff FTEs over that same 20 years (ibid, Page 15) and, of course, you are going to experience a budget crisis.

We are only seeing the effects of this short-sighted ballooning now because, from 2020 to 2024, our schools were being buoyed by the $190 billion in ESSER (COVID relief) money allocated to K-12 education by Congress. Now, finally, we are having to face the reality of the decisions we made in 2018.

Some will highlight that the total share of state money allocated to education has dropped from 51.1% in the 2019–21 biennium to 43.9% in the last biennium. I would counter that the dollar amount of funding has doubled (from $14 billion to $30 billion) in the last 12 years (LEAP Report, Page 19). The percentages speak more about ballooning state bureaucracy than dedication to education.

I run a non-governmental school with no state money. Quality education does not require higher taxes.

##### Rev. Jeffrey H. Moore  Ferndale

##### Editor,

As a 13-year volunteer with Whatcom Hospice, I found Owen Racer’s article recapping PeaceHealth’s Charles Prosper’s presentation of financial solutions to our country’s declines in health care support and funding quite interesting ( [CDN, April 3, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/apr/03/peacehealth-were-working-to-adapt-and-evolve-to-funding-shifts-amid-community-angst/)).

Yes, government changes and the defunding of many health programs have had a huge impact on health care institutions across the U.S. But let me ask this: In light of these challenges, is it a wise _business_ decision to cap volunteer training when volunteer “labor” provides free support to health care professionals who can then otherwise use their time, talents and training for direct medical care? That is exactly what PeaceHealth is doing.

For Whatcom Hospice, volunteers have saved PeaceHealth hundreds of thousands of dollars in salary pay that would have had to go to paid employees to perform such tasks as stocking supply closets, visiting or sitting with patients and families, putting away clean linens, assembling mailings to families of the deceased, providing four hours a week visiting in-home hospice patients and giving in-home caregivers a little respite, doing patient laundry; the list goes on and on. Yes, it takes an administrative salary to oversee a volunteer program. But even if it takes two administrators, it _still_ saves PeaceHealth hundreds of thousands of dollars a year.

I can’t speak to PeaceHealth’s hospital volunteer program, but at the risk of being wrong, I will assume a similar position is being taken. In a previous letter to the editor by retired nurse practitioner and Cascadia Daily reader Margaret Jahn, she pointed out that there are millions of dollars being paid to certain PeaceHealth administrators that seem egregiously out of line. Perhaps some of that money could be redirected to administrators to oversee a thriving “free labor” volunteer pool. Rather than limiting it, how about expanding it? Or, how about let’s bring in another health care provider to pick up the slack? That would certainly free up funds, as no doubt some paid health care professionals would have another employer option.

##### Nancy Grigsby  Birch Bay

##### Editor,

April 16 marked National Healthcare Decisions Day (NHDD **)**, created in 2008 to spark one of life’s most essential conversations: how we want to be cared for when we can’t speak for ourselves. Held the day after Tax Day, NHDD reminds us that “death and taxes” are two of life’s certainties.

PeaceHealth’s Advance Care Planning (ACP) program helped normalize these conversations through education and one‑on‑one guidance. This is the first time in a decade that this resource is not available, a loss that our community deeply feels. People are speaking up, urging PeaceHealth to renew its commitment to meaningful ACP services that help families plan with clarity and compassion.

ACP works best through personal, heart‑to‑heart discussions with family and trusted providers. These conversations build understanding, reduce fear and ensure care aligns with one’s values and goals. The community’s response has been clear: more than 500 residents, joined by the Northwest Washington Medical Society, have urged PeaceHealth to reverse its decision to eliminate the ACP program. Leadership has yet to respond, perhaps believing concern will fade. It will not. We remain steadfast in advocating for what is right and just.

Until this support is restored locally, individuals can still take action. The Known Wishes website offers a free Washington state end‑of‑life planning packet, and the Whatcom County Library System’s “Secrets of Dying Well”class provides additional tools for reflection and planning.

##### Hilary Walker  Deming

##### Editor,

“Off again, on again, Finnigan.” I learned that rhyme at my father’s knee many decades ago; about an old railroad engine that would habitually derail, leading to verbose reports submitted by a track foreman named Finnigan, who, when upbraided by his supervisor for his wordiness, scaled down his reports to the concise line quoted above. Which, after reading about the “C” Street derailment ( [CDN, April 7, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/apr/07/engine-derails-at-roeder-and-c-street-railroad-crossing-in-bellingham/)), I was happily reminded of.

It’s catastrophic derailments that make the news. The airline- and auto-centric public mostly sees modern railroading as long strings of scruffy graffiti-covered freight cars creating delays at grade crossings; along with blaring horns waking the sleeping (and possibly the dead) and the annoying rumble of idling diesel locomotives (such as recently noted by a Sumas letter writer).

During my time working in the track department of the Burlington Northern Santa Fe Bellingham section, occasional derailments would occur, involving a call to the carmen (back then, close hand); who would show up promptly, providing oak blocks and wedges, working with us to set things “on again.” The quicker the better, so as not to shut down the mainline, and we trackmen could get back to other routine tasks; or — since derailments usually seemed to come about right around quitting time — head off to the Waterfront Tavern or Cap Hansen’s. Where those of us who worked on the railroad at ground level might analyze the day’s events.

Certain other bar patrons dubbed us “the low-tech bunch.” Long-gone Mr. Finnigan, I like to think, would’ve been one of us.

##### Paul Kenna  Bellingham

##### Editor,

The cutline for the rendering of the City of Bellingham’s new proposed Civic Complex promenade (CDN, March 27 print edition) starts, “Watch out, grandma!”

I am not sure how to interpret this. Grandmas should not be on promenades with bike lanes? Grandmas don’t belong where there is air ball play? Grandmas don’t like “hustle and bustle”? There are over 90,000 Whatcom County residents age 50-plus (technically old enough to be grandparents), and I am confident most of us will want to enjoy the promenade. Whatever the intended meaning of the caption, this grandma-aged person asks you to consider your wording — and the stereotypes it reinforces — more carefully.

##### Lara Welker  Bellingham

_Editor’s note: Grandmas — and grandpas — are among some of CDN’s favorite people and appreciated subscribers. No slight was intended toward seniors in the caption; instead, the target was the apparently AI-generated illustration used in the city’s presentation that placed a senior in a wheelchair — in a bike lane — with a cyclist barreling toward her._

##### Editor,

Your fine article about Squamish ( [CDN, March 31, 2026](https://www.cascadiadaily.com/2026/mar/31/day-trip-diaries-squamish-b-c/)) neglected to mention the Railroad Museum of British Columbia.

##### Mark Hendershott  Bellingham

##### Editor,

The idea that a Catholic high school should be built in Bellingham with a catchment area of Skagit, Island, San Juan and Whatcom counties must mean global warming is false news. I guess it no longer matters how many prospective students would travel long distances.

The letter from the director of implementation of the proposed high school implies that the Archdiocese of Seattle and City of Bellingham have all the knowledge and our best interests at heart in locating the interim and permanent campuses. Trust the same church that protected thousands of pedophile priests? Trust the City of Bellingham that pays its mayor more than the mayor of Chicago? Not me.

##### Al Lewandowski  Bellingham

##### Editor,

I have, for years, refrained from doing anything about moss on my composition shingled roof. I have a yard full of trees, with a significant amount of various wildlife using them. So, the roof on the north or east sides of my house is covered with moss, with the other sides less than that. I love that moss and the protection it gives to my roof.

There are several causes for shingle deterioration with ultraviolet sunlight as a primary contributor. Most composition shingles are made from asphalt and inert gravel. The gravel wears off and the asphalt dries out and starts to crack and fail. What if your roof is covered in moss? No ultraviolet light, little deterioration.

Doesn’t the moss break down the shingles with their roots? Moss is a bryophyte. Moss doesn’t have any roots. None. Moss grows where their spores land. What moss does, though, is protect your roof by blocking the UV rays, which are a major contributor to shingle failure. So let it land and grow. Obviously, you can stop using moss killer and save our environment, too. And plant more trees and use less asphalt.

##### Craig MacConnell  Bellingham

##### Editor,

More than half of our federal taxes go to the military, which, by the way, has never passed an audit. A $1.5 trillion military base budget for October 2026–27 is an unprecedented handout to tech oligarchs and war profiteers. In addition, Congress is being asked to fund a supplemental $200 billion for the war in Iran.

The Trump administration is siphoning historic amounts of wealth away from everyday families. The president himself admitted this past week that we can’t afford basic investments like day care or Medicare. In addition, Trump is asking for  $53.9 billion for the Department of Energy in FY 2027; $32.8 billion is for the semi-autonomous nuclear weapons agency, the National Nuclear Security Administration. The proposal includes plutonium “pit” bomb core production to the tune of $4.9 billion. Plutonium pits are the essential “triggers” for modern nuclear weapons. The U.S. is now in a race to build up the nuclear arsenal.

Somehow, we need to convey to our government that these expenditures will not keep us safer. Our taxes need to help with basic needs, not enrich a few.

##### Cindy Cole  Bellingham

##### Editor,

Trump never makes mistakes. He thought he did once, but he was wrong. Nuf said!

##### Gene Bogner  Bellingham

![](https://www.pressherald.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/04/43537162_20260409_EPS_5251.jpg?w=1200)Committee clerks pass out papers during an Education and Cultural Affairs meeting Thursday, April 9, for a language review of a bill to reform Maine's school funding formula. (Joe Phelan/Staff Photographer)

Maine lawmakers this week passed the first reform of the state’s widely criticized school funding formula since it was created in 2005.

The bill now heads to Gov. Janet Mills’ desk, and a spokesperson confirmed Tuesday that she will sign it.

The legislation is two years in the making, and began when the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee asked for a study on the formula in 2024. A nonpartisan research group [delivered a report over the summer](https://www.pressherald.com/2025/08/10/maines-school-funding-formula-has-long-been-called-inequitable-changing-it-is-complicated/) outlining potential reforms, which the committee adapted into a bill this session.

The bill is responsive to persistent concerns from school district leaders that the funding formula relies too heavily on property tax valuations to determine how much money districts receive, and does not reflect household income or poverty rates in a district.

[LD 2226](https://legislature.maine.gov/billtracker/#Paper/2226?legislature=132) passed the House of Representatives early Monday afternoon in a 122-23 vote, and was unanimously enacted by the Senate on Tuesday without a roll call.

“The governor believes that every child in Maine deserves a high-quality education, regardless of their zip code. She applauds the Legislature for taking this action on the school funding formula,” spokesperson Ben Goodman said.

Advertisement

The changes outlined in the bill will not take effect until the 2027-28 school year.

During a public hearing on the bill in March, school district leaders from regions across the state spoke in support, calling it an overdue first step to fixing an inequitable, inadequate funding formula.

The final version of the bill makes two significant changes to the Essential Programs and Services, or EPS, formula.

First, it would weigh a district’s economically disadvantaged student rate (derived from the number of students eligible for free and reduced lunch) in the calculation used to determine how much funding a district receives from the state, which is currently based on property tax valuation. Second, it would update an old system of making regional salary adjustments, tying them to a cost-of-living index, rather than a labor market model that has not been updated since 2005.

During debate in the House, several representatives from both sides of the aisle spoke in support of the bill, calling it long overdue and a good step in the right direction.

“It’s something we Down East have been fighting for for well over 20 years. It’s not all we had hoped for, but it’s a recognition that income and economics play a role in the school funding formula, and need to,” said Rep. Will Tuell, R-East Machias. “And I think that alone is cause for celebration.”

Advertisement

However, Barbara Bagshaw, a Republican from Windham and one of two members of the education committee who opposed the bill, said the process had been rushed and that the final bill was missing several of the most important components.

“Yes, it removes some of the more problematic ideas, but it also leaves out meaningful reforms that would have improved fiscal discipline, and it moves forward with structural changes without evidence we need to justify them,” she said.

LD 2226 was [created by lawmakers as a committee bill](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/03/04/lawmakers-draft-overhaul-of-maines-scrutinized-school-funding-formula/) in March, and several components of the bill — including any changes to the special education funding model — were [removed as the committee worked the bill](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/03/19/lawmakers-advance-bill-to-reform-maines-school-funding-formula/) and heard public comment.

The committee passed the bill on March 19, but lawmakers [brought it back late last week for a language review](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/04/09/maine-lawmakers-make-last-minute-changes-to-school-funding-formula-bill/) when the fiscal note came back $30 million higher than expected. After removing some of the provisions driving up the cost, it passed an amended version of the bill 10-2.

The state subsidy and regional adjustment changes will not go into effect for two years, and for the small number of districts that will see a reduction in state funding under the bill, those changes won’t begin until 2031, at which point the subsidy will be reduced gradually over a three-year transition period.

The bill also directs the Maine Education Policy Research Institute, the nonpartisan research group that wrote the report on EPS, to continue studying the formula and provide an update to the Legislature by January 15, 2027.

# OPINION: Fiscal session may prove an uphill battle for school funding



April 15, 2026






It's going to be a brutal fiscal session down in Little Rock as legislators meeting last week and going on for the next month and a half (and maybe more) fight over funding of all stripes.

To the forefront and already grabbing as many headlines as his slick rhetoric can summon, State Senator Bart Hester, R-Cave Springs, and thankfully in his swan song as Senate President Pro Tempore, made his views on homeschooling and private schools versus public schools recently.

Do not misinterpret his words. He really means it.

"We never talk about whether we spent too much on K-12. I will never talk about whether we spent too much on EFAs. It's all educating our children, it's the most important thing that we do."

If, that is, you are a proponent of homeschooling and tax-payer supported vouchers for private- school students.

But don't just take my word for it. Hester, in full frontal zoom made with the TV stations, continues his diatribe.

"If it (the funding of Educational Freedom Accounts, especially designed for home-schooled students and private-school students) goes up $100 million a year, so it does."

And barely able to take another breath before flashing his pearly white teeth at the camera, he continues his personal agenda to enhance the educational experience for students (and parents) who do not want their children in the state's public-school system.

Even a system, led by a handpicked former Florida education secretary, who has been the author of much of Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders' massive, 146-page LEARNS Act passed in her first year in office.

Since the inception of the LEARNS Act, public schools have been regulated to the back burner of any new money or increased significant funding even though mandates on reading levels to qualify students to be advanced from one grade to another are looming to be enforced under the Sanders administration.

And, of course, there is more.

One voice in the legislative wilderness is State Rep. Andrew Collins, D-Little Rock, the House Minority Leader. Here is his immediate take on Hester and increased EFA funding this fiscal session

"The higher we go with the spend now, and the more this becomes ingrained, I think it's really difficult, much more difficult to rein it back later."

And boy, oh boy, is Collins correct.

Locally, and chiming in behind Collins' comments, is State Rep. Denise Garner, D-Fayetteville, who I will interject ran unopposed for the state Senate seat of retiring and term limited State Senator Gregg Leding.

"The governor's budget proposes $309 million in base funding for the voucher program -- plus an additional $70 million in surplus set aside for anticipated growth for a total capacity of roughly $379 million."

Doesn't that alarm anyone? I mean that's a wad of cash not even asked for by these less than 45,000 students (including both homeschoolers and private students). It's like a number someone dreamed up in the Sanders administration that, like all free money offered, will be snapped up.

And why wouldn't it be snapped up by nonpublic entities such as home schoolers and private schools? It is proposed to be out there for the taking of your tax dollars.

Garner continues in a social media post: "To put that in perspective: lawmakers originally appropriated about $187 million for vouchers, then added $122 million more mid-year to reach $309 million. That's nearly $200 million in new dollars flowing into this program -- growing far faster than inflation."

And then comes her chilling statement: "Meanwhile, public school funding is essentially flat in real dollars."

So who are these parents and students who want this increased funding?

Rep. Garner, again, tells us: "And here's the part that often goes unmentioned: more than 80% of voucher recipients were never in public schools to begin with."

So what does this really mean? Again, she writes about the blaring discrepancy in funding, students and dollars.

"About 90% of Arkansas students are still in public schools -- and their funding is holding steady while the voucher program scales toward $379 million."

The only thing I can add is simply this: That $379 million is your tax dollars assessed, collected in taxes and set aside by the state in addition to the tax monies collected for public education that you have a vote on in millage elections, any building projects and expansions.

You, Mr. and Mrs. Taxpayer, have only a vote in the public educational funding, not this Educational Freedom Account payday.

But you do have a vote on those who time after time after time seek to double dip you, the taxpayers, for these extra funds in addition to your school millage taxes.

In fact, the funding of these EFA monies is a tax levy on the state's taxpayers that by and large the rank and file Arkansan did not ask for – and certainly not on the sale of this LEARNS Act and EFA boondoggle proposed, supported and promoted at every stop by our governor.

Once again, 80% of these EFA recipients were never in public schools -- ever.

I well remember the legislative fights years ago on allowing students to homeschool and be exempt from mandatory attendance at public schools. The mantra of those seeking such exemptions promised time and time again -- "We don't want a single dime of tax dollars; we will pay our own way."

Looks like that mantra got dropped in favor of a boondoggle for them.

Maylon Rice is a former journalist who worked for several Northwest Arkansas publications. He can be reached via email at rice4arkhouse85@gmail.com. Opinions expressed are those of the author.
